one_line: Apify's CEO lists x402 agent-payment flaws (double-spend before settlement, HTTP 402 vs MCP 401 conflict, poor fit for metered jobs) and his team's workarounds, including an agent-facing markdown gateway.
summary: Jan Curn, CEO of Apify, gives a sequel to "MCP isn't good yet," arguing that x402 (Coinbase's HTTP-402 agent payment protocol) is promising but has rough edges. He explains why crypto rails suit agent micropayments and walks through the x402 flow: 402 challenge, signed payment, facilitator verification, work, then settlement. The main flaw he shows is a double-spend window, since funds are checked but not reserved until on-chain settlement. He also covers the conflict between the 402 status code and the MCP auth flow's 401, the mismatch between the fixed-fee exact scheme and metered actors, and the upto and batch-settlement schemes. Apify's workarounds were charge-then-refund and an agent-facing markdown site (agi.apify.com) that issues prepaid API tokens. Much of the talk is product promotion for Apify's x402 launch, and the live demo failed.

key_ideas.detail: Payment is verified but not reserved, so the buyer's funds stay usable until on-chain settlement. One wallet can sign many requests. He says this is unsolved in both the exact and upto schemes.

key_ideas.idea: 402 status code conflicts with MCP auth
key_ideas.detail: x402 requires HTTP 402 as the first response, while the MCP auth flow expects 401, and a server cannot return both. A common workaround is a separate hostname per payment protocol, which he calls an anti-pattern. He suggests carrying the payment requirement in a header instead of the status code.

key_ideas.idea: Fixed-fee scheme does not fit metered tools
key_ideas.detail: Apify actors run for seconds to hours and bill as they go. The original exact scheme charges a fixed fee per call, so it fits simple APIs poorly.

They charge a fixed amount under the exact scheme, run the job, then refund the unused balance. It works, but it needs two on-chain transactions, adds settlement time and fees, and requires the client to trust the server to refund.

key_ideas.idea: Upto scheme still leaves the double-spend problem
key_ideas.detail: Upto, announced in x402 v2 (Dec 2025) and shipped about two to three months before the talk, lets the client set a maximum and lets the server charge less. He says it does not prevent double-spending, so they went back to the drawing board.

key_ideas.idea: Batch settlement as a likely fix
key_ideas.detail: The client deposits into escrow, receives a signed voucher, signs off-chain micropayments against it, and settles in batches, releasing the remaining escrow at the end. Apify had not implemented it yet when he spoke.

key_ideas.idea: Why he thinks crypto fits agent payments
key_ideas.detail: Card, PayPal and ACH costs are too high for microtransactions. Chargebacks are a problem with agents because there is no agent identity, so the payment must be one-way. He argues a public, decentralized standard avoids a single company taking fees, and says he is not a crypto supporter himself.

key_ideas.idea: Agent-facing instructions instead of a new API
key_ideas.detail: agi.apify.com is one markdown page that tells agents how to buy a prepaid Apify token (a $5 top-up example). That token then works with the normal Apify API or MCP. Agent instructions can change quickly without breaking the API used by tens of thousands of customers.

key_ideas.idea: Build vs buy flips when token subsidies end
key_ideas.detail: He predicts that once agents pay the full cost of tokens, buying external services will beat building them in-house, and agentic payments will grow sharply. He says the current ~$1M per month volume is small.

techniques.name: Charge-then-refund for metered jobs
techniques.how: Charge a fixed amount up front with the exact scheme, run the job, then refund the unused balance to the client's wallet.
techniques.when: Variable-cost tools on a payment protocol with no safe metered scheme. Accept the extra on-chain transactions and the need for clients to trust the refund.

techniques.name: Work-after-settlement for near-zero-cost calls
techniques.how: Wait for settlement, then do the work and return 200 with a payment response. Double-spend is then harmless for the server, but a failed job leaves the server unpaid.
techniques.when: Calls with near-zero marginal cost, where the risk of a failed job is acceptable.

techniques.name: Agent-facing markdown instructions plus prepaid token
techniques.how: Serve one markdown page that tells agents how to pay. The payment yields a token for the existing API or MCP server, so the payment layer can change without touching the main API.
techniques.when: Several payment protocols are still changing and a large existing API has customers who depend on it.

techniques.name: Batch micropayments via escrow and signed vouchers
techniques.how: Deposit into escrow, receive a signed voucher, sign off-chain micropayments against it, settle in batches on-chain, then release the remaining escrow.
techniques.when: High-frequency small payments where an on-chain write per call is too slow or expensive. Speaker had not yet shipped this.

techniques.name: Local wallet with cryptographic key and QR code
techniques.how: Build a small local wallet tool that holds a key and shows a QR code to fund payments, for testing agent flows.
techniques.when: No ready-made consumer wallet tooling exists for the protocol yet.

numbers.claim: Apify marketplace has about 45,000 tools (actors); community earns over $1M per month in payouts
Coinbase launch added about 20,000 tools to the x402 agentic market (from about 2,000, roughly 10x); launch drew about 1M views
x402 has about 20x the transaction count and volume of MPP, per a check the day before the talk
The 402 status code has sat unused in the HTTP spec for about 30 years
x402 exact scheme launched May 2025; v2 announced Dec 2025; upto shipped about 2-3 months before the talk
Batch settlement scheme introduced about two months before the talk
Demo example: $10 local wallet, $1 allocated for a token, $5 prepaid top-up on the AGI site
Setup takes about 10 minutes for a newcomer; x402 transaction volume is about $1M per month (speaker's estimate)

hot_takes: x402's use of HTTP 402 is good for marketing but a design mistake; payment requirements should travel in headers, not the status code.
A hostname per payment provider (x402.*, mcp.*, mpp.*) is an anti-pattern, like having 20 Amazons for 20 credit cards.
Crypto is the one payment rail suited to agent micropayments, because card rails are too expensive and chargebacks are unworkable without agent identity.
For agent-facing services, markdown instructions for agents can replace a stable versioned API because agents can pick up changes.
Build-vs-buy flips toward buying external services once token subsidies end.

relevance.why: AgentOS L1 has budgets. The talk shows a double-spend race when a budget or balance is checked but not reserved before work runs.
relevance.action: When designing budget enforcement in Govrix Scout, reserve budget before work starts, not just check it, and test concurrent requests against one shared budget.

relevance.why: No content on payments, approvals or harness design that applies to ProsHarness.
Agent payment protocols are not among the recurring interests.
